analysis.one_liner: Would block states and cities from requiring restaurants to pay tipped workers the full minimum wage.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a House subcommittee and died when the 105th Congress ended without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law lets employers count a tipped worker's tips toward part of the minimum wage (the 'tip credit'), paying as little as $2.13 an hour in base wages plus tips. Some states and cities — California most prominently — say no: employers there must pay the full state minimum wage on top of tips. This bill would use federal power to override those state and local rules, capping what employers must pay tipped workers at the federal tip-credit level nationwide.
analysis.who_benefits: Restaurant, bar, and other employers of tipped workers in states and cities that require the full minimum wage for tipped employees. The bill would let them count tips toward the wage requirement, cutting their required base pay from the full local minimum down to the federal tip-credit level, and lowering their payroll costs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would forbid any state or local law that bars a tip credit or requires a smaller tip credit than federal law allows, so employers could pay tipped workers the federal tip-credit wage everywhere [S2][S3].
Federal law already lets employers count tips toward the minimum wage; the bill would make that federal rule override stricter state and local wage laws [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tipped workers in states and cities that currently require the full minimum wage. Their guaranteed hourly base pay would drop from the full local minimum to the federal tip-credit level, shifting more of their income risk onto tips — which vary day to day.

drawbacks.text: Tipped workers in states that require the full minimum wage would lose their guaranteed base pay, because the bill overrides any state or local rule requiring a wage above the federal tip-credit level [S3].

Workers would bear more risk when tips are slow: under the federal tip credit, the employer's required contribution falls to the tip-credit level, with the federal minimum applying only after tips are counted [S2][S3].
The bill preempts state and local decisions to set higher tipped wages, removing local control over a wage standard those jurisdictions chose for themselves [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go to employers of tipped workers, who would save on base wages in states like California that require full pay. The costs fall directly on the tipped workers themselves, who would lose guaranteed hourly income and absorb more tip variability. Supporters would argue a uniform national rule simplifies compliance for multi-state employers, but the bill's effect is a wage cut for a specific group of low-income workers, and it never came close to being weighed on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then sent to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Riggs introduced the Tipped Wage Parity Act on April 29, 1997, joined by six Republican cosponsors [S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction, and about three weeks later to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections [S1][S5].
No further action was recorded; the bill received no hearing or vote before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tipped workers in states and cities that require the full minimum wage kept their guaranteed base pay, since the bill died in committee without a vote. Employers who wanted to count tips against the wage requirement did not get that relief.

for.name: Rep. Frank Riggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would let employers count tips toward the minimum wage even where state or local law forbids it

for.name: Reps. Ramstad, Cunningham, McKeon, Porter, Campbell, and Bilbray

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and the six cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat is listed on the bill, and it drew no recorded floor action either way.

industries.industry: Full-service restaurants and other tipped-service employers
industries.note: The bill would let these employers in states like California count workers' tips toward the minimum wage, cutting required base pay from the full local minimum to the federal tip-credit level and lowering payroll costs. The saving comes directly out of tipped workers' guaranteed wages.
These workers would lose guaranteed base pay at the full local minimum and depend entirely on tips plus the federal tip-credit floor. Their interest runs opposite to their employers' in this bill.
